claims.text: The target material is bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Vacuum sintering can produce nearly fully densified equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Vacuum-sintered HfNbTaTiZr inherently contains roughly 1 wt.% oxygen and related defects.
The oxygen-containing material is a BCC solid solution with minor secondary phases.
The proposed framework combines atomistic calculations, machine-learning corrections, and explicit representations of oxygen interstitials, vacancies, and clustering.
Explicitly modeling non-ideal atomic configurations will improve predictions of thermal and related transport properties relative to perfect-crystal analytical models.
The proposed improvement applies throughout the nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Defect scattering dominates the electron and phonon contributions in the nearly 0–200 K regime.
Oxygen-interstitial effects and phonon scattering predominate from 300 to 1200 K.
Interstitial oxygen produces lattice distortions and defect structures that alter scattering rates and effective carrier mobilities.
Accounting for defect-induced distortions and electron/phonon scattering will make the simulation more representative of real defect-containing microstructures.
At elevated temperatures, both phonon scattering and defect scattering are critical to transport.
The defect-inclusive framework will reduce thermal-conductivity prediction error by at least 20–30% relative to conventional analytical predictions.
At a held-out temperature of 600 K, the framework should predict measured thermal conductivity within ±10%.
Traditional models typically have thermal-conductivity errors exceeding ±30% for this material.
The conventional baseline assumes a perfect BCC lattice and neglects interstitial oxygen and defect-induced lattice distortions.

The approach is limited to bulk sintered HfNbTaTiZr specimens with oxygen concentrations near 1 wt.% and may not transfer to defect-free single crystals or substantially different defect concentrations.
Thermal conductivity will be measured at 50, 150, 600, and 1000 K and compared with predictions from conventional and defect-inclusive models.
The hypothesis is falsified if the defect-inclusive model fails to reduce relative prediction error by at least 20% compared with the conventional model in either specified temperature regime.
